review:
It's only missing a cheat proof online ladder, but the rest is there.
It's a great RPG to play coop with a friend.

Not so great in online games with random people because of tools like TQVault and TQDefiler.
But if you're ok with people duping items and editing their stats and levels without effort then you're good to go.

The game has a huge world to explore which you'll run through 3 times. (Somehow chapter 2 in games is always a desert)
Of course you can call it quits after completing normal difficulty, but you would miss out on some legendary bosses that only appear in the higher difficulties. And all the legendary loot as well, that only drops in the highest difficulty.

I love the art style, I love the landscape, I love the history behind it all. The loot is awesome, you'll fill up your stashes with all sorts of set items in no time. The game has a dual class system which means great replayability. Even the music is good in this game, especially in the final act.

I really like this game and it's probably in my all time top 10 of games I've played. 
And I've played over a thousand for sure.

If only it had a secure online ladder. I think that's the main reason why this game never really blew up.
This original game had a few kinks and hick ups, but now that we have the Anniversary Edition most (if not all) of those are now history.

100% recommend this game.

I btw own the discs as well of the original TQ and IT.
I've played this game well over a 1000 hours.

The game is very long (too long for my taste).
You get more than what you pay for.
I definitely recommend it, even though it has its flaws.

Tips for new players:
- The "A" key only picks up money, potions and artifacts. You have to pick up most loot by clicking on it. 
- If you want to buy a DLC, "Ragnarok" might be worth it, but skip on "Atlantis" (un-optimized junk).
- You can reset skill points, but not stats nor change mastery - you have to download a program to "cheat" in order to do so... or start a new character. 
- If you want to play on higher difficulties, you have to beat the game first, every time.
- If you want to play with mods, achievements won't unlock.

Buy the base game and have fun. If you like it, I recommend the Ragnarok DLC, which adds another chapter to the end of the base game.

Usually i'm not making a review, or if i do it's ain't serious. However this time i'll try to do so.

Alrighty folks, those who played Titan Quest and Titan Quest: Immortal Throne before were quite upset from two things: first since THQ was gone, multiplayer died as well. Second: if you wanted to play TQ:IT you must've installed original TQ as well (logical, yet unpractical).
When Nordic games purchased franchise i thought it was just marketing move, nothing would change. I was wrong, so wrong, lucky for us. Nordic games revived this masterpiece from deathzone and brought multiplayer back to fans. It was dawn of new and long forgotten moment-adventures with friends comes true.

Do you think nothing could be better than reviving old game and bring jolly cooperation to the sunlight? Well THQ Nordic surprised again- they made Anniversary Edition. Combined both TQ and TQIT to just one game, and not only that. They improved and added few things: soundtrack-masterpiece at it was is even better, better HUD, achievements!- now you can proudly show others what did you accomplished, old characters are back!- did you fear you must start the game again even you've level 40 paladin in your old game saves? Fear not, my friend, you can continue your adventure like nothing's changed.
Time to analyze the game.

Graphics: For game made in 2006 graphics are amazing. Beautiful forests of Laconia, dry deserts of Egypt or rocky mountains of Bactria. The enviroment looks fantastic in every corner. Monsters are different to locations- in Greece you can see sathyrs, gorgons (like Medusa), minotaurs and in Egypt you can find some weird mix of men and scorpions,etc.

Soundtrack: It's excelent-changing with situations and i catch myself standing on the ground and just listening this masterpiece.

Gameplay: If you love Diablo styled hack'n'slash with rich story, full of mythology, look no further. This game is definitelly for you. Enjoyable combat and making artifacts can keep you enterntained for hundred of hours.

Another amazing thing is-you can create your own story. You hear right-thanks to map editor you can upload your new quests,location and enemies.

Pros: Amazing story ,beatiful graphics, fascinating soundtrack, enjoyable gameplay, multiplayer, achievements, map editor.
Cons: If there's something bad it's stereotypical missions after time (save guy from monsters, take specifical item from tomb with full of skeletons, or so).

Final verdict-9.5/10 it's Legendary game!

Thousands of hours in both games say this is probably tied with Diablo 2 for 'best Action RPG of all time'
Titan Quest is the lovechild of conventions set by Diablo 2, and the burning passion of talented developers, and the courage to experiment with the formula of an Action RPG. Things like the enemies dropping only what they actually use, which means that you will have to fight for a strong weapon by killing the enemy who's using it, or the fact that the maps are not procedurally generated which means that the developers were able to thouroughly plan and design 'the heroes epic journey' and ESPECIALLY the class system, which allows you to "build your own class" by combining 2 skilltrees (for example, "Hunting" and "Nature" form the "Druid" Class) are the fresh  breeze that I longed for after spending god knows how much time of my life playing nothing but Diablo 2.
From someone who grew up playing both games and therefore put them into direct comparison, I can recommend this game from the bottom of my heart.

Hats off to Iron Lore, and hats off to Nordic Games aka THQ Nordic for the effort that went into the creation of the gigantic patch that is now sold as 'Anniversary Edition', and bringing the game to its former glory.

Short review after completing the game and all DLC on normal, epic and legendary difficulty as a Warden: a phenomenal journey through the ancient world fighting against titans, gods and other deities in this classic ARPG.

Pros:
- Stunning world, environments, lore and locations set in the ancient world (ancient Greece, Egypt, China, Gaul, Scandinavia and other locations all make an appearance with all the mythological lore attached to it)
- Great soundtrack from relaxing town music to pumping combat music you have it all, also while there is not much dialogue in this game all is voice acted
- Superb monster and boss design (all those deities and monsters from ancient lore make an appearance, bigger then life bosses and many monsters from mythical stories with very little re-skins) 
- Combined with all of the DLC a massive and long story with good amount of side quests available focusing on the single-player experience in contrast to modern ARPGS who are league and multi-player focused 
- Amazing loot system (from grey, white, yellow, green, blue and purple item rarity you have it all to make interesting builds), loot below blue rarity can be enhanced with runes while the two best rarity blue and purple can come in a set or with passive/active skills. To spice things up you can also craft artifacts which double down and enhance your builds (bleed, poison, pierce damage and so on)
- Amazing class system in TQ, classes consist of two mastery (for example my Warden has two mastery, defense focusing on skills/passives for armor and shield and hunting focusing on offense skills for spear/bow). With 11 mastery and 66 possible classes there is something for everyone, or if you feel brave you can only play with one mastery and not be a class at all
- Great replay-ability with 3 difficulties and so many classes, loot and even more builds this can be easily an over 1000 hour game if you want it

Cons:
- Some bugs persist, you can get stuck on objects if you teleport away to close to them (press K to re-spawn to fix, items can levitate and not immediately appear on the ground, leave area and return to fix, if you are to close to large objects you wont see your character and your mouse will be clicking on the mountain or object so you wont be moving at all, zoom and try to move then to fix)
- Eternal embers the latest DLC released far after the original game is massive in visual and zone department which pushes the game engine to its limits making it crash after an hour or so, its a ram usage problem, to fix it apply a 4gb ram patch found on forum/guides, slowdowns may still happen
- Main chest is way to small to house all your loot so you either sell your loot, mod your chest or like me have chest alts to hold your booty. With such an awesome loot system the loot filter is weak only able to filter rarity and no additional parameters like sets, stats and so on

What can i say, after almost 200 hours of my journey with my Warden all i can say is this game is one of the best in terms of an ARPG, side by side with greats like Diablo II, Torchlight and Grim Dawn. I can recommend this game to all ARPG veterans and newcomers alike. If you are unsure about the many DLC just wait for a sale and buy them as they are worth it.

As a big fan of Diablo II and its expansion Lord of Destruction, a game that defined my childhood and that of tens of millions of others, I was looking for an isometric RPG with a similar “feel” because I just felt disappointed after so much hype that had been building up before Diablo 3 until the first screenshots were leaked and people started complaining about the wrong direction the visual style had taken, something more akin to the Warcraft universe than the dark and gothic Diablo realm. That’s when I came across Titan Quest that had already been out for a few years. A game set in the Hellenic era, with Act 1 dedicated to ancient Greece. I gave the demo a go and was instantly blown away by the realistic graphics and the visual style not being cartoonish like the Torchlight series was.

The thing about Titan Quest though is – it literally is a Diablo II clone and they are not even ashamed by just how many mechanics they have stolen from it. Which is fine by me because that is exactly what I wanted. 

The story is segmented into Acts, just like Diablo II. NPCs with a quest have a glowing exclamation mark floating above their heads, just like in Diablo II. The checkpoint system (pressing save in the escape menu only saves your inventory but not your location in the game) is made up of rebirth fountains that are basically spawn points for when you die and believe me, you will die A LOT in this game. I died 18 times in total, some of them were avoidable, but far more than I did in Diablo II + LOD. Apart from these rebirth fountains where you can save your progress as you make your way through the wilderness, you then have portal platforms located in major settlements (similar to Diablo II’s waypoints) and portals you can open up yourself to travel back to the town and free up your inventory by selling your loot, again, just like in Diablo II, but with the difference that doing so doesn’t consume a town portal scroll, thus doing away with the portal tome that could keep upto 20 such scrolls. Similarly, the need to identify magical items with a scroll and a tome to store them in has also been done away with, which is a good thing as well. 

On the other hand I feel like rare item drops are far more numerous in TQ meaning you will amass clutter quickly and stop collecting regular non-magical items pretty early on in Act I already as they become utterly beyond useless for the rest of the game. Despite limiting yourself to only picking up and selling magical items, you will amass wealth quickly. 

You have regular items, magical items (yellow), rare items (green) and epic items (blue) that unlike the previous ones, cannot be further enhanced by charms and relics. These in turn come in fragments of 5s and 3s respectively, and you will need to fuse them to create the flawless versions, which can then be used to enhance weapons and armor, just like in Diablo II. Again, the difference is that in Diablo II only certain weapons could be enhanced, ones that had “slots”, sometimes just one, but often several, while in TQ any and all weapons and armor can be enhanced except the aforementioned blue epic items. They also got rid of the Horadric Cube that would fuse your gem shards together (which you can now do yourself by just right clicking on a charm and left clicking on another with the same name to fuse them together) and for the more complicated artifacts, what they did was place a formula guy in every major settlement who can craft artifacts from recipe scrolls you find in the world that require 3 different ingredients, as well as remove charms/relics from weapons and armor (but you have to decide if you want to keep the equipment or the charm/relic as the other gets destroyed during the process). 

Similarly, there is a guy who can help you remove points you have invested into the wrong skills and allow you to respec yourself for a small fee that grows with every additional time you use his ability. This is another improvement over Diablo II as having invested too much into the wrong skill tree seriously impeded your build effectiveness in that game.

There is a health bar and a mana bar, and potions that need to be consumed to keep these high, while Diablo’s rarely used thawing potion to end freezing, antidote potion to end poisoning, and stamina potion as well as the stamina bar have been done away with, which is also a good thing.

What's bad though is that Titan Quest is a faster paced game. Even on the slowest game speed (normal speed), you can quickly find yourself swarmed by a mob or facing a boss who plants a banner or uses an area of effect attack and you are gone in a matter of 5 seconds. In Diablo II, fights were slower, allowing you more time to think and react while here you have to memorize keybindings and use the right skill at the right time in the right sequence to cut through bigger mobs and bosses. The TQ devs know this, and have therefore made dying more forgiving: you lose experience and raise a tombstone that you can then reclaim to get back some of your lost xp after returning the area and clearing the monsters, while in Diablo II you dropped all your gold and all your gear which was hilarious.

Another thing that sucked in Diablo II was you had to pick your hero before you even began the campaign, and if you were new to the game you wouldn’t know what style of play you’d basically be forced into for the next 50 hours. Spear and bow amazon, staff sorceress, dual wielding barbarian, shield and aura paladin, you know... but in Titan Quest, you only have to decide if you want to play as male or female. From there on out, you are given the choice to select two classes some time during Act I and this can be ANY combo, heck, you don’t even have to choose a 2nd class and can postpone this until much later, instead spending the attribute points you get after each level to rise in your primary class much faster. So there’s warfare (melee weapons), defense (shield), ranger (bow), nature (wolves and forest nymph archer girl accompanying you), rogue (assassin), dream, and different elemental classes for mage builds. But like I said, you can combine pretty much anything. My first and only complete TQ playthrough (I’ll explain why in the next paragraph) for example was nature and warfare (dual wielding weapons, even though I also used a bow as secondary backup), dubbed in the TQ community as “the champion destroyer”. This uniqueness and mix-matchability of builds adds immensely to the replayability of this game, because picking completely new classes feels like a true breath of fresh air after…. 

80 hours. That’s right. The TQ main campaign and Immortal Throne expansion together take that long to beat, it is truly a yuuuge game. I started playing this game in 2012, and by the time I had finished Act 1, I was so sick of it I gave up for the next 8 years, only to come back in 2020 and do all acts out of sheer determination. In 2012 I had picked warfare and storm, but in 2020 I went with warfare and nature. Seeing your wolves and nymph accompany you felt a lot more like playing with other players; a multiplayer "party" which kept me going through this extremely long game that would have otherwise been dreadfully boring if I was all by myself the whole 80 hours. The story is…meh…okay, kinda interesting, but nowhere as spooky as following “the wanderer” in Diablo II. The weird creature you saw in the intro video is called a Telkine, and there’s actually several of them, and they are the primary factors of chaos in the TQ story as they go about to set in motion a series of events that will lead to the end of the gods.

Is TQ worth playing? Yes, if you have lots and lots of time to kill. Like during quarantine! But at the same time, want a game with a story and an ending and not an eternal cash cow like Path of Exile. Therefore, go for it.

I've played thousands of hours of POE, played the original Diablo when it came out, played most other ARPGs out there.  Titan Quest is my favorite ARPG.  The class trees feel legitimately distinct and interesting and itemization is great.  The voice acting is full of character and top notch.  And the setting is easily (by a very long mile) my favorite of any ARPG:  most ARPGs love their dark, grimy setting, but after you play a few of those, they just are hard on your eyes and feel quite dull.  Titan Quest is bright and cheerful without being cartoony, and really makes you feel like you are in Clash of the Titans.  Yes, it's slow compared to modern games, but the production values are high even compared to a lot of contemporary games, and TQ still plays very well.  There's even new expansions out (which I hear are mostly not that good) if you are looking for a game that is still being worked on.  If you are a fan of the genre, this is definitely a game you need to play.

This game is 10 years old, and it seriously still holds up. You could release this today and it would still be better than most other ARPGs, which probably explains my unscheduled dropping of the other games I was playing to put 18 hours (so far) into this! In fact, as much as I love Grim Dawn (and acknowledge that it's a "better game"), I still prefer Titan Quest. Its ancient mythology setting immediate differentiates it from the demons, doom and gloom of most other ARPGs, and it's so refreshing to play through the bright sunlit Greek hills once more. It makes the contrast with the darkness and the musty caves that much more striking.

And has anyone ever done ragdolling better than this game? Smashing creatures in the face and watching them sail over buildings and disappear into canyons is still enormous fun, and later on it's like being Sauron in the prologue to Fellowship of the Ring. Lighting up the screen with spell pyrotechnics also looks fabulous with this edition. I love the combat in Titan Quest (once it gets going), which is probably a good job because it's a long game.

It's not perfect. Titan Quest always had a slow start, NPCs love to blather on about stuff in faux-Greek accents if you keep clicking on them (completionists be warned!), and it's a few hours in before you really start to feel like a warrior. Good job then that they've introduced a speed setting to whisk you past the opening and onto the good stuff. Once you upgrade your movement and attack speed, you'll probably want to turn it back to normal to keep up. There are other little touches, like a new "pick up all collectibles" button which saves a lot of clicking. Multiplayer also finally works again, and coop in Titan Quest is a hoot.

The biggest improvement for me, though, is that the playfield now scrolls smoothly and without any of the annoying blurry judder of the original. I installed TQ on half a dozen PCs and I could never get rid of it, so having it scroll around silkily at last is a massive difference and improves the feel of the whole game. Whatever they did (triple buffering?), it makes a beautiful game look modern again.

So yeah, thanks THQNORDIC for bringing us these improvements, and giving it to existing owners for free. Hopefully it will allow more people to discover this classic.

Titan Quest is a classic of the ARPG genre and is regarded by many as one of the few games to measure up favourably against the juggernaut that was Diablo II. With the improvements of the Anniversary Edition, and the new release after 11 years of a new expansion in the shape of Ragnarok, can it still stand up against the new kids on the block of the genre? This is what I think of Titan Quest.

Titan Quest can still hold its own today, yes. Despite aging in some areas and not having some of the comforts and QoL in some newer titles in this genre, the gameplay is still rock solid. It also benefits in being truly unique; no other game like this has the setting in Ancient Greece and beyond. It's steeped heavily in mythology and as someone who is fascinated with the time period, it's magnificent. 

Much as the trend in ARPG's, the story is fairly limited in favour of the gameplay. After creating a hero, with an extremely limited character "creator," you end up on the outskirts of Helos, a small village in Greece. The village is under attack by monsters, namely Satyrs. This is happening all over Greece, and it's up to you to hack and slash your way through legions of monsters, drowning in seas of loot and blood towards saving the world. It's undeniably epic, especially towards the end of the base game. A decent offering. 

In terms of gameplay, it's still very satisfying. Watching creatures ragdoll when killed is strangely enjoyable and the combat is great, if repetitive at times. Completing quests, killing monsters and collecting loot is the order of the day here, and as you level up you can put points into 9 skills trees, or masteries. Once you reach level 8, however, it gets much more interesting. You can then choose a second mastery and mix and match between them, or just stick with one. This opens up great replayability, and is only bettered by Grim Dawn in my opinion. I've only played as a Conqueror and Ranger so far but I want to play many more. 

The level design is just exquisite. I'm not really a fan of dark and gloomy and Titan Quest is such a breath of fresh air. A wide variety of maps and different vistas, along with varying monsters as mythologies change is a far cry from the depressing worlds of Diablo and Grim Dawn. Ancient cities, old tombs, temples, forests, mountain passes, deserts and the very gates of the Underworld itself make for a rich world. There is also plentiful checkpoints situated throughout, so you can generally play in short spells or long sessions too. I cannot talk highly enough of this game. 

Graphically, it still looks decent even after 12 years. It can't match newer titles but it's certainly good to look at, especially the environments. The aforementioned variety in levels also helps the game immeasurably, ensuring you don't grow bored of the same thing over and over. The soundtrack is also incredible throughout, changing with each act when it suits. I've heard some fans gush over the voice acting and it's solid, but I wouldn't call it amazing. They do a decent job overall.

Negatives. There's always negatives. Progression and combat in Titan Quest is slow. Play Torchlight II and notice how much faster it plays. I grew used to it and came to like it but I like faster paced combat. There's not enough storage options for a game like this, making the creation of a legion of mule characters something of a necessity after a few playthroughs. Movement is not as smooth as something like Torchlight II or Grim Dawn, and certain cave sections could be annoying to fight in. Another pet peeve is the gold problem. By the time you are done, you'll have millions of gold pieces jingling in your pocket, and buying things from traders is ludicrously expensive to match. Not a big deal, just something that both bothered and amused me. I also would have liked to have seen more customisation of your character, like in a favourite of mine, Torchlight II. Anything to make your hero a little more unique other than what colour of tunic they're wearing. 

So to cap it all off, I liked this game very much. After bouncing off it a couple of times after finding it a little boring, it really came into its own on my third attempt and what an epic ride it was when I had finished. With it's addicting gameplay, fantastic masteries system and unique setting, you won't regret this classic romp through the Ancient World of gods and monsters. ARPG fans need to at least try this one, it's quite good.

TQ AE stands tall when compared to other releases of that era. It's not Diablo 2, but probably the only game since that really understands what it takes to keep you engaged or even excited to be smashing the same content over and over again. The Anniversary Edition adds some welcome quality of life upgrades in better resolutions, a setting to adjust game speed (crucial!) as well as bug fixes and overall balancing of items and classes. With an at-the-time original multi-class system that allows you to create the exact character you want and a loot system bursting at the seams with things to collect, you wont find it hard to spend a couple...hundred hours romping with the old gods. If you missed it the first time around, Titan Quest is a bonafide classic and with the recent cleanup to multiplayer, makes for a good co-op game to play with your normal pals even if only between modern releases.

I used to play this game when it was originally released. I have fond memories of waking up early in the morning (age 17), getting my breakfast cereal and preparing for a day of non-stop immersion into a world of ancient mythology.

Returning back to it now (at age 29), I am amazed at how well this game has aged. It's still relevant and still as enthralling as the days I spent playing it when I was younger. Sure Diablo III and Torchlight II were just as awesome in their own right but I think the nostalgia I have attached to this game just makes it way more memorable to me.

I started playing it again 4 days ago (after realising it's STILL getting new content OVER 10 YEARS LATER) and I already have 55 hours of game-play. I've since purchased the Ragnarok expansion and look forward to playing the new act but I'm loving all the awesome new things they've added, not to mention, it's been remastered!

It runs like a dream on my, average at best, laptop. Even when set to full graphics!  Maps are not randomly generated which allows them to be beautifully crafted and visually stunning, plus, you get to know them really well for doing loot runs. Best of all, there are no loot boxes, no daily achievements, no pay-to-win problems and can be played by myself at my own pace. I love that!

Definitely a must have for anyone who likes playing aRPGs or even anyone who enjoys mythology for that matter (the story-line and voice acting is really epic and well researched).

At the price point, this is a total steal.

Its actually funny: Playing Titan Quest in 2025 feels like playing an early version of Grim Dawn (my, by far, favorite aRPG)
Titan Quest is a fun game even though it feels a bit more "simple" than Grim Dawn and more whacky at some points

"A timeless journey forged in myth and mastery."

I've played Titan Quest since its original release in 2006, and to this day, it's one of the most enduring, immersive, and rewarding ARPGs I’ve ever experienced.

What makes Titan Quest: Anniversary Edition stand out even now—decades later—is not just its rich blend of mythology, storytelling, and exploration across ancient civilizations, but the sheer depth of mastery combinations and build creativity. For me, this isn’t just a game—it’s part of my gaming DNA. If you're even thinking about trying it, know this: your legend begins the moment you pick up that first weapon.

"More than a game—this was my myth, my childhood, my legend."

Long before the age of battle passes and paywalls, Titan Quest gave us something rare: a world to lose ourselves in, with no strings attached—only sword, shield, and destiny.

I've been with this game since the very beginning. I was one of the kids who stayed up all night theorycrafting builds, discovering mastery synergies, hunting for that one legendary drop, and memorizing the routes through Egypt and Olympus like they were sacred.

Titan Quest: Anniversary Edition isn’t just a remaster—it’s a time capsule. And yet, it still holds up. In fact, it thrives. With the added expansions and quality-of-life upgrades, it feels like a gift to those of us who never let go—and a rare treat for those discovering it for the first time.

[h1] The Review [/h1]

Love ARPG’s of old when it was much simpler time. When there was no auction house for loot debacle, when ARPG’s were all about acquiring the loot the old fashion way. Killing a bunch of monsters and feeling how powerful you will get. When it was all about being a bad ass with tons of stats info about how much damage your legendary weapon can inflict. Behold old school ARPG’s fans Titan Quest is one such game that might be able to quench your thirst by replacing killing demonic hordes with killing mythology creatures. Only lacking is a good story but that is not what you are here for, it’s all about being powerful and sending my Liche King to suck the living daylights out of my enemies.

Titan Quest made by the now defunct Iron Lore entertainment has always been a sort of diamond in the rough with ARPG’s. Its story was not all that entertaining and overall was a very repetitive game like most ARPG’s but it had a way of making you feel powerful with ton of experimentation with its classes. ARPG’s at times can be a bit of grind but classics like Diablo 2 showed the appeal of the grind can be immensely fun at times especially in the later stages. Combine that with unique visuals, interesting character classes, abilities and lore. You might just have a great combination for a good RPG like the classic Diablo 2. On the other hand, Titan Quest delivers on the gameplay front not so much on the lore or plot but before we head to the nitty gritty stuff let’s get to the story. Titan Quest story is very simplistic as you create your character and go about your journey to stop the Telkines, a lesser Titan of sorts. These lesser titans’ wants to release Typhon, a powerful Titan to wage war with the Gods in Olympus by summoning monsters and as usual humanity is being caught in the crosshairs. There is a secret organization along the way that helps you in your journey but to be honest the story is there just to push you forward.

Where Titan Quest truly excels is giving you ton of unique classes to experiment with powerful abilities making you feel like you are God of War chosen disciple. Having a total of 36 classes combinations including the generic warrior, archer, and mage builds, that is a ton of builds to wage war. I went with the spellbreaker combining my passive leeching abilities with the warrior more offensive build. And I have to say despite the lackluster plot and somewhat barebones lore in the beginning, I had a blast fighting all manner of legendary beast. Ranging from beastmen, Minatours, undead like mummies, harpies, insects, automatons, terracotta warriors and more which adds quite a lot of unique visual enemies design despite most of them playing quite identical at times. Enemies charge and try to swarm you, while most of the time you time your attacks and abilities to have a bit of strategy in controlling the horde. There is always a range unit among the horde of melee enemies attacking you. Occasionally you will bump into a few bosses which will throw some unique abilities like fireballs at you or stop all your passive abilities. There are side quest but it never is anything interesting and mostly standard ARPG fetch or kill quest. Go there kill this monster or go there and fetch that item. The story for these side quest are also really not that interesting. 

The early game is honestly the weakest aspect to Titan Quest where enemies often do the same thing and that goes for almost two acts set in Greece and Egypt before it hits the third act in the Orient which I assume is China. This also applies to the loot giving you a ton of crap you do not need. The third act on wards is honestly where the game shines, with enemies throwing a bunch of abilities, fighting various types of enemies all at once, and of course better loot. Enemies are often forcing you to time your abilities and at times spam at the potion buttons. Bosses are also really good in the third act onwards often providing good loop and interesting encounters such as facing the Terracotta Sorcerer which constantly throws terracotta warriors your way while attacking you from a far. The side quest and lore gets much better once you reach the excellent immortal throne expansion which is a blast to play. At times it feels like the early sections were the early access while the last two acts are the final product.    

Visually Titan Quest anniversary edition is still pretty to look at despite its age, there is a ton of variety on the enemy designs to the locations, from Greek theaters and temples to giant pyramids and sand dunes and finally the Great Wall of China. Overall it’s all really decent looking although sometimes the forest and swamp areas is a bit hard to see with trees occasionally blocking your view. However I feel the Hades regions are some of the much more interesting locations showing a ton of interesting environments on the afterlife. Floating souls like streams over ash like sand dunes and volcanic environments to ruin like cities. It’s quite a sight to behold for such an old game. There has been some slight graphical overhauls but nothing major and its a nice touch. The sound design is honestly nothing to shout about. Voice work isn’t great and music is sparse most of the time. So you will be hearing a lot of the same hitting and screeching sounds depending on what creature you kill. Sometimes the voice work is honestly atrocious especially in the Orient and Egypt region. There are some minor bugs like getting stuck after teleportation. 

With that being said, the main appeal of the core ARPG loop is what Titan Quest does best. And I would imagine this game would be a blast to play with friends. There is a ton of replay value if you want to collect powerful relics, loot and try all the classes’ unique variety as well as abilities. It is though a more slower game than Diablo series where at times it does not allow you to just rush in but instead forces you to retreat and fight smart in the later stages. It is a shame that the pacing feels a bit lackluster but Titan Quest Anniversary Edition overall delivers. Combine with the excellent Immortal throne at least the game is fun in smiting the titan hordes and quenching your thirst for some old school ARPG. A big thanks for the publisher and developers for giving this game free to whoever owns the original base games.

I started playing this game because Grim Dawn was bumming me out -- i'd do something magnificent, vanquish some super powerful evil demon, then the game world would react with a "Yeah, great, he's dead and all, but we're still ROYALLY fucked." This is not to Grim Dawn's discredit, as they were really going for a bleak tone and nailed it, but sometimes I just want to feel like a badass and a solid homie for doing justice. 

That's where Titan Quest comes in. It takes the whole "one person against an army of demons, monstrous animals, and questionable big-titty fan-service baddies" thing, and delivers it in a way that's a lot more hopeful and lighthearted. 

I also find that the too-much-loot-at-once problem i run into with some other ARPGs is absent as well -- drops are more rare than, say, Grim Dawn or Diablo 2, but that also means i don't have to sort through a mountain of what basically amounts to trash, just to find the salient items. Itemization is fantastic, and having items of a lesser rarity that can, in some cases, completely trump items of a technically higher rarity...it just feels great and serves to encourage utilization of whatever comes your way, and lessens reliance on BIS items -- and makes the journey to getting those items a bit more bearable. 

Over the last few months I've played nearly every big time ARPG in this vein that i could find, and Titan Quest is a contender for best of them all, in my opinion. It just FEELS good to play. Highly recommended.

[b]PROS:[/b]
+ epic feel of the campaign
+ ancient mythology
+ cool boss fights
+ tons of loot to pick up
+ 9 classes (+1 with Ragnarok DLC; +1 with Eternal Embers DLC) 
+ fun co-op (online needs registration)
+ nice soundtrack
+ Immortal Throne expansion included

[b]CONS:[/b]
- Steam Cloud issues
- memory leaks/crashes to desktop
- some issues with Alt+Tab
- glitchy animations
- some unbalanced enemies/heroes/bosses
- not all skills are worth using
- somewhat repetitive/bland item models

[b]Comment:[/b]
As someone who played ARPGs from Diablo 2 up until (the current version of) Path of Exile I can see what we gained in modern ARPGs. The original game is old and because of that it was missing many quality of life elements (auto-heal in town). The Anniversary Edition adds something (even more with the Ragnarok DLC and EVEN more thanks to Atlantis & Eternal Embers DLCs) but not a ton.

Gameplay may seem a bit sluggish but you can adjust this in the Options. Just put Fast or Very Fast in the game speed section. Incremental additions to skills are both good and bad. It boosts some skills and makes them great. Others stay in the dust and are barely usable. A small percentage to trigger on many skills means they are often useless in boss fights. The maps are static and the only dynamic things are shrines, chests and enemies. Sixteen(!) resistances divided to primary and secondary can be overwhelming and honestly too much to balance. I advise to invest into Vitality resistance early on and always keep some swap gear with various stats for specific monsters/bosses.

Sometimes you run into a "roadblock" when you meet a hero monster or boss that you need to either respec/re-equip for ... or just cheese it. This feels awkward, especially if you're a melee character and need to switch to a bow or spells. You can argue that difficulty is good but this is more the case of design. And it doesn't feel fun to have to suddenly switch from how you want to play. Some balancing would have been good.

Also worth mentioning is the classic loot tiers depicted by different colored names and the three difficulty levels. I really liked the original TQ along with the Immortal Throne expansion, mainly because I like classic action RPGs like Diablo 2 and Torchlight 2. This "remastered" edition is missing some stuff to make the game more modern but it still is loads of fun, has TONS of content and is worth getting.

The base of the game is the Ancient Greece, when the humans were protected by gods; but the they are in danger because of the Titans who broke from prision and want revenge against the gods.
You are a unknow warrior who after save a small city you are asked to look for help, it makes you travel through Greece and later on Egypt, Babylon and China as the only one who can defeat the Titans. That being said, the creation of bosses and equipment based on each region's culture it's really amazing, giving most gods something to represent them.

[h1]Main features?[/h1]

-The game doesn't has a character customization, your options are male or female and you can choose the color of your tunic. However, the game gives you a astonish number of armor for your head, chest, arms and leggins, also you can wear rings and amulets. There is also a posiblity that enemies drop relics and charms that you can assemble and attach to weapons and armor to give more stats to them. Besides that, most of the stats are random and yo can find the same piece of armor but one with +100 health and the other one with +100 mana, so you can choose the one that best fit your gameplay style or to improve the one thing you are lacking the most 

-You can choose a Mastery between 8 possible and later on you can choose a second one or stay as you are. It gives you the oportunity to have 36 different combinations with unique abilities. Also, every Mastery has a really balanced skill tree, giving you the opportunity to choose whatever you want and don't fell powerless at all.

-Each Mastery has 20 skills (40 if you choose a second one) that you can unlock and improve 6-12 times each.

-The amount of weapons you have is insane, based on your Mastery, its strengths and weaknesess you can wield swords, knives, axes, cubs, maces, bows, spears, or staffs, with different stats (some of them are random). Also, you can use anything if you have the requeriments for it, it can make you a Necromancer-Hunting who wields a big ass axe with no restriction at all.

-It has a pretty decent pet system, the AI does a good job and if they are doing it wrong you can change their target to that big fat monster that is killing you.

-Now it has Mod Support and thanks god it exist. If you somehow manage to use all the Masteries or you get bored with them there are some great mods with all-new, all-diferent classes and some useful tool for your grinding.

-If you want to have all the achievements you will have a hard time, to begin with, each playthroughis last +60 hours and with a achievement for every difficulty-mastery one, is good to say that many of them have a achievement rate of 1.0% or less. Good Luck with it.

-MULTIPLAYER!!
The main and best feature, you can play with your friends in custom quests and add as many mods as you want (it helps you to level up faster). Also the health of the enemies and the damage they deal changes with the level and number of players of your party.

I have been playing this game since it came out in 2006, before even Immortal Throne was announced. I was 9, and had to share the computer with my mom and younger brother.

Let me tell you, this game is STILL AMAZING. Yeah, the engine has hiccups, but I'm amazed it still runs on newer machines. My whole family played this game RELIGIOUSLY, and when Immortal Throne was released, we bought it immediately and played it for years. It brought my family together during some of our most stressful times, to be honest. 

Since then, seeing that it has STILL been updated and added on to? That makes me so very happy. I never thought I'd see people getting to experience just how amazing this game is, let alone get to see new classes and content added on.

If you're looking for a technical review, here it is:
You'll have to mess with settings to keep it from crashing or developing huge glitches. It's an 18 year old game, what do you expect?
Gameplay is a lot like other ARPG's, especially with the class-mixing system and skill point allocation. It's not super "innovative" if you've played other ARPGs. But you have lots of story, rich lore, and gameplay time.
Performance? Hypothetically speaking, if one were to steal a computer from your local high school (that probably is still running Windows XP), you could run this game just fine with it. It takes next to nothing to run the game. It runs on 1 singular cpu core if that tells you anything, and (unless you mod it) doesn't even approach using 4gb of RAM. doesn't matter what video card you have either. your CPU could have integrated graphics and this game wouldn't skip a beat.

Please give this game some patience, and love. Iron Lore and THQ Nordic deserve tons of respect and love for not only bringing this game to Steam and every other console, but updating the game and adding DLC well over a decade later for the players who loved this game before and continue to love it now. I feel like a happy kid again being able to play this game. And as long as the developers give this kind of love to the next iteration, I'm hoping that one will be played decades from now as well, maybe even by my kids.

I'm very definitely biased, don't get me wrong. But I'm sure you'll like this game and I hope you keep it alive.

This is perhaps one of the best ARPGs I've ever played. Just to give some history, I've Played Diablo 2, 3 & 4, Torchlight 1 & 2, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing 1, Grim Dawn, and Path of Exile. This one is right up there with Diablo 2 and Path of Exile. Actually, it's better than that IMO because of the quality of life improvements and my personal pet peeves which this game doesn't trigger in the slightest.

This game isn't tedious, which means no back tracking unless you're really trying to farm a specific type of mob. Respawn points don't take long to get to, which means when you quit and mobs respawn, you don't have to run through them to get to where you want to go because you'll be right there. You aren't wandering around a zone for hours in repetitive terrain trying to get somewhere specific which is helpful if you have to quit the game in a hurry. 

Titan Quest won't overload you. Each area has about 2 optional quests that you won't have to go out of your way for to complete. Usually, you'll complete them easy with map exploration or on the way to your next objective. Speaking of exploring, so far the entire map has been seamless (other than getting on a boat and traveling to a new area). No loading screens when entering a dungeon, settlement, etc. As I mentioned before, unless you quit and reload, monsters stay dead.

The skill trees for each class choice are unique, engaging, and executed well. You won't find them in any ARPG you've played before. Not to mention there are a lot of builds that work well with one another.

Now let's talk about the negatives as compared to other ARPS: Well, there really aren't that many. You can make the argument that the game play doesn't feel fresh and the graphics aren't on par with other games of this genre, which is fair considering the date when Titan Quest was first released. With that said, if you still enjoy Diablo 2, you'll enjoy this game as it improves upon it in so many ways. Just to be clear, most of the ARPGS I've played are more recent than this, yet there is a reason I'm playing Titan Quest and not the other games I've mentioned.

The only real negative I have for this game is the dialogue. For whatever reason, the written dialogue scrolls faster than the voice acting which annoys me. If that's where you draw the line, then oh my god don't play this game, it will end you!

Titan Quest does the genre justice. If you enjoy ARPGS, this is a must play, a hidden gem even as it's often overshadowed by the Diablo franchise and Path of Exile. I was going to wait until I beat it to leave a review, but the first 15 hours has been so fun, I couldn't help myself. This game is worth your money regardless of whether or not it's on sale.

I first played Titan Quest when it originally came out, and have returned to it several times in the past decade. In many ways, it is outshone by more recent ARPGs, but it still has a charm that many of those lack. Since it's impossible to avoid comparisons in a genre where there is so much similarity between titles, this review is going to focus on what I think Titan Quest's particular strengths and weaknesses are, relative to other more recent ARPGS.

- The easiest comparison for Titan Quest is to [b]Grim Dawn[/b], as it was made by many of the same folks. The skill and class systems have a lot of overlap. Grim Dawn includes deeper character customization in the form of the Devotion system, but the two-mastery system is conceptually the same. There are even a few skills that are effectively (and even named) the same, like Heart of Oak. Grim Dawn also includes a more robust endgame, with a few different options for high level farming (compared to TQs much more limited selection). Overall, Grim Dawn is mechanically deeper.

- [b]Path of Exile's[/b] gem system, extremely complex passive tree, and continuing development make it the dominant player in the current ARPG market. Many of its strengths, however, are also its weaknesses relative to TQ. PoE is best enjoyed when participating in (usually) 3 month leagues. If your time is limited, it can be difficult to 'finish' a character in such a league, and ongoing tweaks to the passive tree mean that a character you had high hopes for becomes impossible to build after a patch. Furthermore, it's essentially impossible to build a strong character in PoE without trading with other players. The economy of each league is, in my opinion, a lot of fun and a strength of the game's design - but if you're more of a single player it may not be for you.

By comparison, TQ (and Grim Dawn) are very single player friendly; you can start a build, leave it alone for weeks or months or even years, then come back to it and be right where you left off. It is possible to trade with others or play multiplayer, but if you're going to do that, I would honestly recommend PoE or Diablo, as they're really built for that. For SP, TQ and Grim Dawn are definitely my go-tos.

- I haven't played much [b]Diablo III[/b] (and I wasn't particularly crazy about it when I did), but I'm going to group it with another ARPG, [b]Torchlight[/b], because of its feel. Both have a cartoonishness to the art style that I personally don't find very appealing. Blizzard, of course, is famous for its toony approach to art assets, and Torchlight is intentionally a more light-hearted take on the genre as a whole.

I think feel is where Titan Quest really shines. Grim Dawn and Path of Exile are both have a dark, grungy, post-apocalyptic feel that, frankly, ends up feeling very same-y to me. I play PoE for mechanics, competition, and complex character building, but I've never felt invested in the world or the story in any meaningful way. Similarly, Grim Dawn failed to grab me in the way that Titan Quest did, despite its improved complexity. Diablo and Torchlight's cartooniness, meanwhile, didn't grab me either.

Titan Quest, meanwhile, draws heavily on Greek, Egyptian, and Eastern Mythologies (though, let's be real, they do a way better job with Greek than the others, which can be a bit token-ish). For a classics nerd like me, the setting of TQ has always been a draw. The whole game world is beautiful, and there are so many clever touches and references that I keep discovering with each new playthrough.

For example, after killing the Cyclops Polyphemus you'll be rewarded with a 'Majestic Chest,' a common reward for killing mini-bosses, and an achievement called 'Nobody did this,' which is a clever reference to the name Odysseus gives when he kills Polyphemus in [i]The Odyssey[/i]. You can also go into a small cave behind Polyphemus, expecting more loot, but only finding a couple spiders and, maybe, a small chest or two, often with a skeleton holding onto it. This reference to the barrenness of the Cyclops's cave is a subtle reference, again, to [i]The Odyssey[/i], and it shows how carefully constructed the whole world of Titan Quest is.

TL;DR - If you're looking for a good single player ARPG and think you would enjoy a bright, colorful, mythology-infused setting (that avoids being cartoonish), definitely consider giving Titan Quest a try. It has held up well, and still offers plenty of fun even 11 years after its original release.

Back in [b]2006[/b], I [i]totally[/i] loved [b]Titan Quest[/b]. For many reasons. I always loved the genre (played and finished most of the games in it, even those that are barely known), I always loved [b]Greek Mythology[/b], the game had pretty nice visuals, while the overall atmosphere was bright and charming, which was a nice distinction from our usual [b]Diablo[/b] clones. It was a really nice game for all [b]ARPG[/b] fans to enjoy. Unfortunately, there was a huge problem with it. And the name of that problem was multiplayer. It didn't have the most basic features (like [b]Ladder[/b], for example), it was way too easy to cheat there and the worst of all – online multiplayer was based on [b]GameSpy[/b]. Yes, yes, [i]that[/i] [b]GameSpy[/b]. The one that ruined a lot of good games just to ultimately die one day, leaving all those games without any multiplayer at all. Some games (like [b]Total War[/b] series) fixed the problem in updates. Some others (like [b]Crysis[/b] and [b]Command & Conquer 3[/b]) just pretended that dead multiplayer isn't really a problem (hello, [b]EA[/b], I hate you too). Unfortunately, [b]Titan Quest[/b] ended up in the second group. So, years later, I was really happy to hear that there's going to be an updated and improved version of the game. Especially since publisher claimed that all owners of the original version will get the new one for free and there'll be a totally new expansion soon. Sounds great, right? Especially since we don't get new games in this genre that often nowadays. What can go wrong? Well... everything. Everything can go wrong.

First of all, I kind of don't get the point of separate new version. Most of the changes here are just some little tweaks. Something that you can expect from a regular update. Multiplayer is back (obviously, without [b]GameSpy[/b] now), they've made it a tiny little bit harder to cheat there (would work in [b]2006[/b], doesn't really work nowadays), [b]AI[/b] was improved a bit (hard to notice), there's a proper [b]Steam[/b] support with [b]Steam Trading Cards[/b] and achievements now and, of course, there are more resolution options and alternative [b]UI[/b] for high ones (which I totally liked since I have a pretty poor eyesight). All that is pretty neat, of course, but totally not enough for a proper new edition of the game. The only [i]really[/i] good thing here is mod support. [b]Steam Workshop[/b] is [i]always[/i] a good thing. As long as your name isn't [b]Bethesda[/b] and you don't try to sell your silly stuff there. There isn't much mods for this game yet, but... it's always nice to have mod support, right? Unfortunately, there's one thing that pretty much ruins all the fun. And that thing is... balance. Makers of this version completely re-balanced the game and oh... my... [b]God[/b], they pretty much ruined it.

And I'm not talking about the fact that some damage types feel extremely weird on high difficulties and can even lead to [i]a lot[/i] of cheap deaths. My biggest problem is the loot. Remember how fun the original [b]Titan Quest[/b] was? At the end of the [b]Normal[/b] campaign, your whole inventory was full of blue items and it was fun to find something new and interesting after the every single boss encounter. It was really fun to inspect and compare all that cool loot. Remember that? Now let me give you a simple example. In this version, even when I've beaten the final boss of the new chapter from new expansion / DLC on [b]Legendary[/b] (highest difficulty in the game), I've got only... yellow loot. That's right, the most basic yellow loot that's pretty much worthless. After killing the "big and scary" final boss. Now here's a question – [i]what the heck?[/i] The whole purpose of high difficulties was to get a good equip. Now even on highest difficulty the drop is, like, one hundred times worse than it was on [b]Normal[/b] in the original game. Why? Yes, it makes you grind. For hours, for days, for weeks, for months and so on. But the thing is... [i]It was a freakin' [b]2016[/b] already!!![/i] Which means that there was more than enough games in the genre, there was [b]Path of Exile[/b], which provided far better experience, there were all those [b]MMO[/b]s that provided much more rewards for grinding, etc. All that ultimately killed the entire player's motivation to keep playing. Like, there was no [i]reason[/i] to grind so much in a [b]10[/b] years old game that doesn't even look better. See, [b]Square-Enix[/b] got the right idea about that when they've added those in-built cheats in their old [b]Final Fantasy[/b] titles. They totally overdid it, yes, and I totally didn't like the way they did it, but they've got the right [i]idea[/i]. Re-playing an old game that wanted you to grind for months back in the days may not be as fun nowadays. Now, makers of this version not only didn't get the right idea, they actually made it way worse than it was. Which means that this game... it just isn't as fun as it used to be anymore. It totally isn't.

And, of course, there are all sorts of smaller problems now. Let me just give you a short list of those. In this version some of the extra items that were obtainable through external codes were removed with no explanation. Most of the major quest bugs weren't fixed (all those half-broken scripts are still there, so, it may take a few re-runs just to make a certain quest work, even if it's a main quest). There's a really weird loot-related bug when almost every time you get something better than regular yellow loot, you get the same exact item soon after it. The whole game feels like it was re-balanced in favor of the DLC and the changes it made for classes, so, even though importing your old character from physical copy of the game, or the old [b]Steam[/b] version will technically work, you'll probably suffer a lot. Most of the time it's even hard to get the right drop for your class. For example, even though I tried to play as my old [b]Conqueror[/b] I've made in a physical copy of the game, the only loot I've got was the one for magicians. Which I wasn't even able to wear. The new expansion / DLC sucks and comes with absolutely awful level design (it's hard to even see where to go, for example) and ridiculously stupid (and sometimes frustrating) quests. Some of which also want you to grind. Like you didn't have enough of that already.

The list goes on and on and on, but the only thing you should [i]really[/i] know is that it's a pretty much broken version of the good old [b]Titan Quest[/b]. And I'm not talking about the fact that times have changed and playing [b]Titan Quest[/b] nowadays isn't as fun as it used to be. At least because there are way better alternatives. For example, my biggest complain about the [b]Grim Dawn[/b] was that it still felt a lot like [b]Titan Quest[/b] and some of the [b]UI[/b] features and game mechanics felt really dated and rusty. All that is true. But the biggest problem with this version is – the original version of [b]Titan Quest[/b] is still more fun than this. Even though there are mods now and multiplayer actually works, the original [b]Titan Quest[/b] still provides far better and more enjoyable experience. Just because it doesn't feel like frustrating grind fest. In a freakin' [b]2016[/b]. Dixi.

Probably in the top 3 of best ARPGs I've ever played.  Often considered the predecessor to Grim Dawn this game uses the (if done correctly) amazing class system of choosing two separate masteries to create your class. There is a lot I could say about this game but I'm going to start off with the negatives first.

-The Cons- 

1. This is not your modern ARPG

Before anyone jumps on me and calls me out for not being a "true" fan of the genre or anything, I actually PREFER this. I LOVE that this game is not your modern, 1 button pressing, legendary loot at level 10, inconsequential builds ARPG. This to me is NOT a negative but it must be stated because if you are NOT interested in putting at least 10+ hours into this game you probably will not see what I see, and 10 hours is kinda low to be honest. I will get more into this when I talk about the classes/builds but just know you probably won't feel like a "strong" or "special" character for a much longer time then you'd be used to coming from modern ARPGs. Couple this with the hard bosses (Typhon WILL stop your run the first time you playthrough, that's fine, enjoy it, start a new character if you'd like, don't stress), rare loot drops, most abilities have cooldowns unless meant to be your autoattack, and you're going to be drinking potions like your life depended on it because it normally does.

I know this is a negative point but I must say from my perspective I'd really give this a try still. The bosses are meant to be slow burn events, loot is meant to be exciting when you get it (and many people have beaten the game with yellow, or uncommon, only gear), ability management USED to be a part of ARPGs and I'd wager the genre has gotten worse for moving away from this, and while drinking endless potions can be annoying 'E' and 'R" are your best friends.

2. Quality of life

While MOST of the quality of life features I can overlook the two I cannot defend is the game "remembering" what difficulty you last played on (many times I accidentally play on Normal with my Epic+ characters). Speaking of I'd actually commit ARPG blasphemy and say that APRGs SHOULD move away from the 3 difficulty system, while I understand the point of it and don't MIND the idea of running older zones with harder mobs, I just think forcing the player to "start over" 3 times is quite archaic. This is admittedly very minor but it is very annoying, however this game also ESSENTIALLY has no stash and this is a genuine concern.

The stash system in this game is SO extremely minimal that if you have even 2+ characters and would like to keep gear for either future runs or just for any sort of collecting you will run out of space probably by Act 3. There are work arounds TQ Vault is a great resource after I ignored it for years I now use it all the time. This is definitely a genuine complaint with the game that I can't defend or argue against.

-The Pros-

1. Classes/Builds

Arguably every ARPG lives and dies by its classes/class system. I could probably write a 100 page thesis on why classes are important for ARPGs but this isn't about that, it's about Titan Quest, just know that I cannot understate how important it is to have a compelling class system and Titan Quest definitely does. 

So this game has a total of 11 masteries, with DLC, you as the player at level 2 choose your first mastery that can be leveled up to 40 with new actives and passives after leveling up your mastery. Once your character has leveled up to 8 you choose your 2nd mastery which then creates your class. While your class doesn't generally affect any stats (masteries do 'class' doesn't) most people understand what you're trying to do when you mention your class (for example if I say I'm playing a Conqueror veterans understand I'm probably building auto attack heavy character).

All this to say, just surface level, there's a lot of playstyles, but then I'd even argue each class has multiple niches to them. Want to play an archer with a lightning orb pet? You can. want to play a trap placing dual wielder? You can. Want to play a fire mage with wolves? You can. (disclaimer you CAN not saying all these builds can push Eternal Embers Legendary, I simply don't know)

Then we have.

2. Itemization

The gear/class system of this game makes SO MANY interesting combinations of fun things to do. I remember the moment I fell in love with the itemization of this game was the moment I found a shield (can't remember the name, sorry veterans) that had a chance to on block create a huge temporary pet ON a character that used shields and pets. There's many examples of this but especially in Epic+ there's many items that will seemingly validate your builds you've been working on. 

Again, loot is rare and specific loot is even more rare, but there are so many items out there that validate dozens of different builds to at least make it TO Legendary, probably further. 

5. Everything else

From the setting, to the enemy diversity, to the boss battles, to the heroic monsters, to the massive content available. This game truly is special and as I said before is top 3 ARPG of all time with a MAJOR argument it could be number 1.

P.S. I hope TQ 2 is half as good as this.

You will probably spend a lot longer than you anticipated getting through just the first difficulty even if you're trying to power through it, and especially if you explore side-areas, do all the quests and play through all the expansion content.  This could be a good or bad thing, but I'll note it as a positive, but it leads me to my first negative point below.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
 - [b]Exhausting.[/b] As stated, it's a LONG game.  Like, really long.  Kind of too long.  It's going to take you DOZENS of hours to get through no matter what you do.  And 95% of that is going to be spent slavering through trash mobs with your small handful of active skills of choice over and over and over.  Even if the game itself is well-crafted, this will get grating.
 - [b]Linear.[/b]  As opposed to almost every other 'Diablo clone' out there, you're not going to see any randomized areas here.  The trash mobs in any given area may be slightly random per-run as dictated by a small pool of possibilities but most of them and all major bosses and minibosses will be set in stone, as well as all the areas and placement of chests and such.  This will make replays even more tedious when combined with the aforementioned game length.
 - [b]Difficult.[/b]  More than simply challenging, this game starts easy enough but borders on ludicrously, unfairly, overly difficult as you reach certain milestones of the story.  And this is just on NORMAL difficulty, and before even reaching the expansion areas.  It's going to be virtually impossible not to feel like an absolute glass cannon on all but the most ridiculously tanky builds, and the sheer amount of different stats you will need to pump to feel truly defensively strong (an over-abundance of elemental resistances, defensive ability, armor, hp, etc) is way too extreme.  It's also easy to find yourself in a situation where you're not dishing out enough damage, even if you made wise stat and skill decisions and have decent equipment.  You may have to depend on OP builds or grind for especially powerful equipment to be able to pass certain chokepoints of difficulty.  These three negative points combine to make replayability a chore, even if it's nearly outweighed by the sheer fun of trying different classes.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Titan Quest is still a good hack n' slash and worth playing if you like the genre, especially Diablo-likes.  Just be prepared for a LONG slog and bring friends if you can.

The Anniversary Edition was just a great reason to revisit this incredible game. Solid and competent Hack-n-Slash, if you're tired of Diablo and Path of Exile, I'd say this should be your next choice if you want some more H&S.
So what's good about this game? First, its obligatory H&S gimmick is its classes. You have a choice of 9 classes, of which you can take two, which gives you 36 possible class combinations, and all of which have viable builds with good synergies, you're not gonna be just an archer or just a fireball-throwing mage - you can be an archer who also casts storm magic, or a fireball mage who's also good at getting surrounded and tanking hits with his shield while blasting monsters with AOE.
The second fun gimmick is enemy drops - anything that your enemies wear, you can pick up and wear too, and on the other hand, if an enemy has a legendary weapon, you'll experience its effects on yourself. It does not add that much to the game, and the ground will be littered with garbage equipment you wouldn't even think of picking up, but it sometimes does lead to interesting situations and adds a tiny bit of emergent gameplay.
The game is pretty for its time, and does not look half-bad today. The environments are vibrant and diverse (except for dungeons), and you'll be traveling all around the world from Greece to Egypt to Babylon to China to Greek Heaven to Hades. Monsters and equipment will also be changing according to the region where you encounter them.
Now about the things I don't like about the game. First, it is too long, around 25 hours to finish the game once on easy. Medium and Hard act like New Game+ and New Game++, so that's maybe 50 more hours to reach the end-game content. The game has artifact crafting, and for that you need to farm for specific randomly-dropped legendary equipment, which will add up to a lot more hours. With this game having 36 class combinations, they could have made its pacing faster so that you'd be able to experience as much of the game as possible, and even if you're fine with touching only the basic classes, that's still 5 playthroughs. The game absolutely does not have enough content to warrant replaying it so much and for so long, especially considering the map layout is static, it is not generated randomly. You will have fun with your first playthrough though.
Second, the plot is about NPCs throwing boring scrolling textboxes at you (they are voiced though), there's really nothing interesting about it, no deep concepts or anything, the lore is a very sparse retelling of ancient mythologies, and the characters are dull static NPCs with historical or mythological names floating above their heads.

My review may be a bit biased because I absolutely loved this game when I first played it.  Playing it now brings back a lot of wonderful memories.  It is an action RPG/hack and slash game in the same vein as games like "Diablo"  And as such I'll be comparing it a lot to the Diablo series and similar games.

PROS:

-You can automatically sort your inventory.  Anyone who played Diablo I'm sure remembers how annoying it was to constantly rearrange your inventory piece by piece every time you heard that you couldn't "carry anymore".  With a click of a button you can auto sort.

-The graphics are still impressive given its age, the backgrounds are dynamic, and there is a change from day to night.  You travel to cities, beaches, catacombs and forests.  You aren't just stuck in one type of area.  Also the graphics look more realistic and less "cartoony".  No "gore" means parents can rest a little easier having younger gamers play it.  The ragdoll mechanics are hilarious and never gets old.

-Any lover of Greek mythology will enjoy fighting centaurs, harpies and the like.  It is similar to "Prince of Qin" when it comes to using a lot of mythology lore for its creatures and settings.

-You walk right into caves instead of waiting for a load screen.  I for one, think that's pretty cool.

-There is a staggering number of different "builds" or masteries you can try depending on your play style.  There is the ability to respect your points which makes it so you don't feel like you wasted time on a build you don't like.  You can start customizing your character very early in the game.  And you are able to hotkey various spells depending on your character builds.   You aren't limited to picking just one of two spells in a particular tree to use.  


-Your characters have a multitude of stats and resistances.  The gear you are able to wear is based on your stats.  You can't be a mage class and just thow on heavy armor.  

-You know right away what base stats your crafting components add.  You are not just breaking down equipment and praying to the RNG gods.  You do get random bonuses on top of your base crafting stats though, as well as the ability to reclaim your craft component to use again in another item.

-You have an ability to use a town portal vs. having to carry a half dozen town portal scrolls in your inventory.

-The music.  Seriously go find the "secret passage" and enjoy.  It's not the same "doom and gloom" track over and over again, but each piece fit the areas well.  

-Level creation option and modding capabilities.  Multiplayer is there but there is also a legit play singleplayer campaign.  Not "singleplayer if you are able to log into battlnet" singleplayer.  

-No microtransactions, auction houses or other cash grab bs.


 CONS:

-Grinding/Farming.   In typical ARPG fashion you will do lots of grinding and farming.  

-Linear gameplay.  You do have multiple difficulty levels, but the game itself is a linear experience.

-The music is awesome, but in a lot of places it's few and far between.  You'll be playing and wonder "where did the music go?"

-Enemy AI - depending on the mob you can just walk right up to its back and start wailing on them before they even know you are there.  Sometimes you walk right into a room full of enemies and it takes them a moment to even acknowledge your presence and start fighting you back.  This doesn't happen often but it is worth mentioning.

-The levels, including the dungeons are not randomly generated.  Which isn't a con for me but may be for other people.

-No real character customization...unless you use mods.

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
Titan Quest’s ancient Fantasy setting, spanning from Greece to African regions and even higher planes of existence such as Hades (Hell) and Elysium (Heaven), is overall detailed, consistent and well-made visually and artistically. Despite its age, the visuals hold up well enough, and the ragdoll physics add some dynamicity to an otherwise very static combat feel. If you enjoy historical settings, you’ll feel right at home. 

Given that deep, meaningful plots are never a priority in this genre, efforts have been made in other iconic titles to, at least, grant a semblance of interest to the various tasks at hand, take Diablo II for example. That doesn’t happen in Titan Quest, however. Whereas the main story is generic but serviceable, any and all side characters or quests are inconsequential—their middle school grade writing only worsens the dullness of tasks already repetitive by nature. You’ll find no interest whatsoever in any of the admittedly iconic characters you’ll meet, such as great ancient heroes and even demigods, all stripped of any pathos or epicness they may have had.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore each area on foot, your only means of transport besides two-way portals that allow fast-travel to discovered locations, such as cities, to sell loot, use facilities and restock consumables—the standard ARPG fare. Notably, quest givers aren’t highlighted when it’s time to return a completed quest, so good luck remembering where “Generic NPC I Forgot The Name Of’’ is located. The average speed of your character is inadequate to traverse any area in a decent time; with how large each map is, you’ll find yourself walking more than fighting, since enemy density is subpar. You’ll often ask yourself when the current area will end, because you’re fed up with it already.

Each map has plenty of side-areas and dungeons that often host Elite or Boss enemies guarding higher-tier chests that have a chance to spawn the best loot. Exploring is worthwhile to mop up as much XP as you can, but not so much for loot since most chests, including “secret” ones, have miserable rewards. The satisfaction of finding a secret dungeon, clearing it and getting some actual good loot from it is almost always absent.

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
The combat gameplay, of course, will change based on your Masteries (classes) of choice, ranging from pure casters to summoners, melee specialists, archers, rogues, and why not, a mix of all the above. The amount of combinations is staggering, with a relatively cheap respec option available at any town for skills. The standard ARPG system of mana, health and related potions is in place, plus an array of consumable Scrolls that have a variety of unique effects, purchased for a high price or rarely found. Should you perish in combat, a feat not easy to achieve due to the generally tame challenge posed by your foes, an XP penalty is applied, having you return to your death-mark to reclaim it; nothing else is lost.

The cooldowns. Good lord the cooldowns. Of any ARPG I have played, Titan Quest takes the cake for the slowest, most infuriating cooldown timers. Whoever thought a 30 seconds cooldown on the basic Taunt skill for a tank (which doesn’t work properly half the time anyway) or even 60 second ones on caster skills were good ideas, should take a break from game development and play some Diablo II to see how it’s done.

Even if the enemy variety is good in a general sense, most maps overextend and bloat for too long, having you fight countless of the same fodder far past what would be ideal for this genre. The Elite and Boss enemies aren’t unique or meaningful enough to grant the needed diversity. Speaking of higher-tier enemies, unless you go against one that is twenty levels above you, you won’t have much problems dealing with them, at least on the default difficulty setting. Most of them are miserable, generic, and just don’t stand out enough from the crowd save for some different color or aura around them. I died a total of five times in the whole game, which isn’t a lot. 

[h3]Character Progression[/h3]
By killing enemies and completing quests, you’ll level up and receive 3 Skill and 2 Attribute points each time. You can also get these as quest rewards, alongside other unique bonuses like +% damage, but that’s a rare occurrence. 

You’ll also loot charms from enemies and chests, which can be used on weapons to bestow passive traits that compound your build, and also reused by destroying the weapon to get the charm back and then put it on a better one.

Leveling up in Titan Quest is tremendously slow: by the end of the campaign, after doing everything, I was just level 37; the level cap is 75. That’s less than one level per hour, which may be fine for the last 10-20 levels in an ARPG, when your build is already shaped up, but it’s a depressing affair so early. Your gameplay evolves slowly, frustratingly so: your combat experience will stay the same for hours on end if you decide to focus on a few skills, which is the only way to make them worth using to begin with. Also, you’ll also have to spend skill points to increase your Mastery level and access higher tier skills, further sinking more points into passive stats instead of active skills that evolve your class’ gameplay.
